en: Every block of a language model has one express lane running past it. What if you built four?
And how would you keep four lanes from blowing up?
Start with one lane. A transformer is a tall stack of blocks: attention, then a feed-forward layer, again and again, dozens of times.
Each block doesn't replace its input. It adds a change on top: x plus F of x. The plain x is an express road. The block is a town you exit into, and its result merges back onto the road.
Why does that matter? Training sends a correction signal, the gradient, backwards from the last layer to the first. Her example:
The express road has no gates, so the gradient rides straight down it. ResNet made this shortcut the standard, about ten years ago.
Without it, the signal would pass through every block in turn, like a message whispered down a long line of people. By the end, it is mush.
The second thing a deep stack needs is normalization: shift and scale a group of numbers, so they average zero, with a standard spread. But which group?
BatchNorm, from image models, measures each feature across a whole batch of examples. Like a tailor measuring the waist of everyone in a row.
LayerNorm measures one example at a time: all the numbers of one token, head to toe.
Sentences come short and long, so batch averages wobble. LayerNorm needs no batch at all. And her slide is honest about the real reason: experiments show it works better.
Modern models trim it further. RMSNorm skips subtracting the average, and has no bias. It only rescales.
In its 2019 paper, it matched LayerNorm's quality, with 7 to 64 percent less running time, depending on the model. The Llama family uses it.
Now the real question. Where on the highway do you put the toll gate?
The 2017 Transformer added first, then normalized. That puts a gate right across the express road. This is called Post-LN.
Every gradient has to squeeze through every gate. In 2020, Xiong and colleagues showed that Post-LN starts training with large gradients near the output, so it needs a slow warm-up.
Pre-LN moves the gate onto the exit ramp. Only the copy going into the block is normalized. The road itself stays untouched.
Pre-LN can train without warm-up and reach comparable results. BERT kept the original Post-LN. GPT-2 moved the norm to the input. Her slide's verdict: only earlier models, like BERT, used Post-LN.
Her point is that the names mislead. What matters is not before or after. It is whether a gate sits on the express road.
One more idea: normalize what goes into the block, and also what comes out, before it merges back. Two gates, both on the ramp. The road stays clean.
This is Peri-LN. Gemma 2 and Gemma 3 do exactly this. OLMo 2 uses a close cousin. Models shipped it in 2024, and a paper studied it in 2025.
A norm is cheap next to the big matrix multiplications, so an extra gate costs little.
So far, one road. The residual shortcut itself had barely changed in ten years. Then she asks:
Hyper-connections, from Zhu and colleagues in 2025, copy the stream into several lanes, here four. Each block reads a learned mix of the lanes, and writes back into all of them.
The block itself still runs once, so the expensive part costs the same. Only the cheap merging gets richer.
But now the crossovers have weights. Her toy example: if y is x1 plus x2, each input gets the full gradient back.
If y is 0.2 x1 plus 0.8 x2, the gradients come back scaled, by 0.2 and by 0.8. So the weights decide how much signal gets through.
Learned, they worked. In the paper's big test, the model reached the baseline's loss 1.8 times faster, counted in training tokens.
Here is the catch. Those weights multiply, layer after layer. A weight of 1.1, a hundred times over, is about 13,800. A weight of 0.9, a hundred times over, is about 3 in 100,000.
A snowball, or a whisper. When DeepSeek measured plain hyper-connections, the signal gain through the stack hit about 3,000.
Their fix is called mHC, from Xie and colleagues. It puts one rule on the mixing. Picture four jugs pouring into four pots.
Every jug pours out exactly what it holds: each column sums to 1. Every pot ends up with exactly one jug's worth: each row sums to 1. Nothing negative. That is a doubly stochastic matrix.
And here is the trick. Multiply two of them, and you get another one. Her slide checks it with real numbers.
So stack a hundred layers, and the total mix still obeys the rule: the mixing itself can never stretch the signal. Measured, the gain stays near 1.6, not 3,000.
With one lane, the rule leaves just the number 1: the plain shortcut, back again. The price is about 6.7 percent more training time, with four lanes. Their main test model has 27B parameters.
Her slide has the best picture of all this. Attention is a person in a meeting, listening to others, learning whose words matter more.
Hyper-connections are one person with four clones, talking among themselves. Same token, a richer picture of itself, deeper in the network.
One honest limit: the 1.8 times is counted in training tokens, on one model. Clock time is another question.
So: deep models train because every block adds onto a clean road, and the gates stay off it. Now the road can have lanes, as long as every mix keeps its rows and columns at 1.
Next time: the knobs we set before training.
